subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
passage: Dear diary, I'm Diya, and today was strange. Ma'am taught us how to divide fractions: "flip and multiply." Easy! I did all twelve sums in the book and got every one right. I don't know why you flip. But it works, so who cares? Then she wrote a word problem on the board. A ribbon three-quarters of a metre long is cut into pieces one-eighth of a metre each. How many pieces? I stared. No sum, only a story. Which one do I flip? I guessed and I was wrong. Ma'am said, "Think about what the question means." I don't know what it means. Tomorrow I'll ask her.

qa.q: How many sums did Diya do in the book?
qa.a: Diya did twelve sums, and got every one right.

qa.q: What was Diya feeling when the word problem appeared on the board?
qa.a: Diya felt lost and worried. The familiar rule did not help when the question came as a story.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Diya use to understand dividing fractions, and why?
qa.a: Diya could cut a paper ribbon into eighths and count how many fit in three-quarters. Seeing the pieces would show why the rule works.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see Diya's mistake on the word problem?
qa.a: Ma'am probably sees that Diya knows the rule but not what it means, which is why Ma'am asked Diya to think about the meaning of the question.

grounding: A child learns flip and multiply without understanding why, gets familiar sums right, and is lost when the teacher gives a word problem in a new shape.
